newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua armed gang wary of government peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua armed gang wary of government peace talks.

text.p: The leader of the largest armed gang remaining from Nicaragua's civil war said on Wednesday his men were ready to keep fighting if the government does not bargain in good faith in upcoming peace talks.

In one of three government-designated "peace zones" high in Nicaragua's rugged northern mountains, gun-toting rebel commander Mario Jose Herrera, known as "Little Bird," said his men were willing to talk peace but were wary of government tricks.

They were ready to disarm "if the government does not turn its back on us or try to trick us," Herrera, a former Contra guerrilla who now leads 60 re-armed rebels, told CBS-Telenoticias in the town of Ayapal, Jinotega, 209 miles (334 km) north of Managua.
Herrera said the recent election of right-wing President Arnoldo Aleman, who took power on Jan. 10, partly motivated his right-wing gang to be willing to talk peace.
"We know that he is a man of maturity and responsibility, a democratic man," he said.
Former President Violeta Chamorro referred to the armed rebels as "delinquents," discounting their political claims.
Nicaragua's civil war ended in 1990, but many former combatants later re-armed to protest the government's failure to fulfil the terms of the peace treaty.
The army estimates that 500 members of 33 armed bands loosely linked to the former Contra rebels or Sandinista army continue to operate in northern and central Nicaragua.

Despite repeated government amnesties and help to reinsert former combatants into civilian life, the problem has not gone away. Since 1990, armed bands have killed 1,000 people, wounded 400 and kidnapped 600 civilians, according to army figures.
Aleman has promised to disarm the gangs, who kidnap and rob farmers and ranchers, creating insecurity in the countryside.
Late on Tuesday, Aleman issued an ultimatum to the gangs saying they must take advantage of the government's offer to negotiate their re-insertion into civilian life or face the weight of the law.
Aleman, with the support of the army and police, said it was the rebels "last chance" and called on them to assemble in one of three "peace zones" to begin negotiations.
